Messages.Author: George Fink
Messages.Body:
A few questions on self-contesting:

1. Is it possible?

2. Can you yield one copy at the start of your turn and then gain the
use of the other copy for that turn, or do you have to wait a full
time around the table?

3. When you yield to yourself, do you play 1 blood for the copy you
keep?

--George

Messages.Author: L. Scott Johnson
Messages.Body:
In article <GFINK.96J...@avalon.cs.ucdavis.edu>,

George Fink <gf...@avalon.cs.ucdavis.edu> wrote:
>
>A few questions on self-contesting:
>
>1. Is it possible?

Yes. (Errata to the VtES Rulebook).

>2. Can you yield one copy at the start of your turn and then gain the
>use of the other copy for that turn, or do you have to wait a full
>time around the table?

If, during your untap (after you've yielded/contested all of your
contested cards) you have the only reaining copy of a contested card,
then you gain control of that card. You do not have to wait
for another trip around the table.

>3. When you yield to yourself, do you play 1 blood for the copy you
>keep?

Yes. (Or you could yield both copies).

As I recall, according to Tom's answer to this same question on this
thread, you _do_ have to wait until the following untap to gain access to
the card. I can see arguments either way -- it's really a timing question.
One could say that since the card hadn't been yielded at the start of the
untap phase then it remains face down until the following untap. On the
other hand, one could argue that since the contesting card is yielding at
the start of the untap, the other card should become available at the same
time, since it is still the "start" of the untap.

What I really suggest is that you and Tom agree on what the correct answer
is! :-)

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
The rules state that if all but one copy of a contested card is yielded,
the remaining copy comes back during its controller's *next* untap phase.
Whether it's currently that player's untap phase is unimportant; the
card still can't come back until the next untap phase.

Messages.Author: Zaphod Beeblebrox
Messages.Body:
L. Scott Johnson (lsc...@crl.com) wrote:
: In article <GFINK.96J...@avalon.cs.ucdavis.edu>,
: George Fink <gf...@avalon.cs.ucdavis.edu> wrote:
: >
: >A few questions on self-contesting:

: >
: >3. When you yield to yourself, do you play 1 blood for the copy you
: >keep?

: Yes. (Or you could yield both copies).

Why? The moment the first copy is yielded, the second is no
longer contested. In addition, except for a few cases, and in
Jyhad at least, you can order the events in any given phase
however you wish, yielding one card and then another, for
instance, rather than dealing with both simultaneously. Under
these assumptions, then, one copy would be yielded and the
second would be instantly usable with no cost.

-Dave Green

Hopefully, Tom and I already agree. You have to wait until all
other copies are yielded. If you are contesting with yourself
(only), then this should be at your next untap. When you yield
(and pay one for the other), you do *not* have to wait for yet
another untap to come around before you get control of the card
you just wrested from yourself.

Your turn T1: influence phase: contest a card with yourself.
Your next turn T2: untap: pay one contest and yield the other.
At the end of your untap phase, turn the copy you paid to
contest face-up and place it in your controlled area.

You do not have to wait until the following untap (of turn T3)
to regain control of the vampire.

I interpretted Tom's "next untap phase" statement to refer to
the untap phase of T2. If this is not the case, and it is
easy to interpret it the other way, the I appologize for the
confusion. TOM?

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
Zaphod Beeblebrox <dc...@faraday.clas.Virginia.EDU> wrote:
>Why? The moment the first copy is yielded, the second is no
>longer contested. In addition, except for a few cases, and in
>Jyhad at least, you can order the events in any given phase
>however you wish, yielding one card and then another, for
>instance, rather than dealing with both simultaneously. Under
>these assumptions, then, one copy would be yielded and the
>second would be instantly usable with no cost.

That would work if the rule about recently-contested cards was "If a
card is no longer contested during your untap, it returns to play."
But the rule is actually "When a card is no longer contested, it
returns to play during its controller's next untap phase." If you're
currently in your untap phase, then the card doesn't return until the
untap of your next turn.

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
page 37, Vampire rulebook:
"If a previously contested card ceases to be contested, you return the card
to the active region, face up and untapped, during your next untap phase."

Note "at the end of an untap phase", but during one. No exception for
the card being yielded during your untap phase. If a card stops being
contested, you *must* wait until your *next* untap phase; if you're currently
in your untap phase, that means the untap phase of your next turn.



Hate to show up late for this dance, but I understood that it was not
only silly but illegal to contest your own cards.

LIke I have a Sarah Cobbler in play with a nasty master card (like
Vampiric Disease or something) so I want to get rid of that one. I
have another Sarah in my crypt and bring her into play.

Since "controlling" the vampires in your crypt is like recruiting and
there is only _one_ Sarah, how can I recruit her twice? This is like
saying, "Yes, I know you play for the St. Louis Cardinals, but we want
you to play for the St. Louis Cardinals!"

I understand the process of bringing a vampire from your uncontrolled
region to your controlled region to be the application of a certain
amount of influence of the Methuselah to a particular individual. I
further understand how another Methuselah may use her influence to
give that individual doubts and make the individual "working for
nobody."

I fail to understand how I can convince somebody working for me that
they should work for me...again. And thereby actually work for nobody.
If this isn't cloning, I don't know what is.

Messages.Author: Brian Kallenbach
Messages.Body:
**I think you folks know what this thread is about by now...**

Come on people, vampires in your crypt are "minions who you hope to control" (from
Darkness Unveiled.) As a Methuselah I highly think it would be utterly stupid and
completely daft to think "Hmm, Sarah Cobbler has a Vampiric Disease. Maybe, I'll go out
and use my Dominate powers again, and get a Sarah Cobbler without a disease." Or, "Hmm,
Sarah Cobbler has a Vampiric Disease, maybe I'll go ask her to join me again, that
oughta get rid of her disease." Or, "Hmm, Sarah Cobbler has a Vampiric Disease, she
doesn't want this miracle cure I can give her, so I'll pose as another Methuselah,
because I need her to kill off all these other Methuselahs." As a Methuselah, if a pawn
of theirs contracted or came into the posession of something that would harm the
Methuselah, that Methuselah would probably say: "Hmm, Sarah Cobbler has a Vampiric
Disease, well, she can't do me much good, now, better send her off to Alamut to stir up
some trouble with them Assamite fellas," and go about his business as Sarah was
slaughtered.

Point being, Methuselahs are vampires with tremendous resources (as vampires go). And,
when one of their minions becomes a liability, they don't go out of their way to help
them, they send them on a suicide mission on which they have no chance of coming back.
Then go out and find a suitable replacement for Sarah.

It ain't that important people, why don't we just drop it and move on to bigger and
better things?

Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:
On Thu, 27 Jun 1996, Brian Kallenbach wrote:

> Point being, Methuselahs are vampires with tremendous resources (as vampires go). And,
> when one of their minions becomes a liability, they don't go out of their way to help
> them, they send them on a suicide mission on which they have no chance of coming back.
> Then go out and find a suitable replacement for Sarah.

If the Methuselah felt Sarah was important, it would use its influence on
her to make her better. Influence doesn't necessarily mean recruitment.
In a Jyhad game-world sense, Influence has nothing to do with
recruiting. These vampires might not even believe you exist, so how do
you recruit them? Simple. You don't. You put into play mechanizations
so that they do what you want, whether they know you are their
puppetmaster or (more likely) not. One of those mechanizations
(contesting your own) means, in game terms, that you are taking a much
more serious interest in that minion. If your interest result in the
curing of a vampiric disease, this is not a big surprise.

When talking about game balance, this too is not a problem. You are
spending to bring out the card (whether in pool, influence, master
phases, or actions), do not have use of the card for a full turn, and
then have to spend a pool on your next untap to keep it. There is no way
this can be considered abusive.



The simple fact is Methuselahs DON'T have huge enough resources to
simply dispose of vampires whenever they get screwed up. What you
described is more like Antediluvian behavior. Finding a suitable
replacement isn't always as easy (or as quick) as just fixing the problem
in whatever roundabout way the methuselah decides. Observing (drawing
from your crypt) and recruiting (influence) a brand new vampire is slow,
wasteful, and expensive. An efficient and prudent Meth. would either take
the time to resolve the condition of a useful vampire that has been
victimized by your rival or would find a way to make the most of the
situation if nothing could be done.
